title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 11–12
description: Curated B2 vocabulary about housing, household objects and chores, routine domestic faults, minor injuries, practical repairs and everyday mishaps.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Teaching themes and vocabulary were checked against the source; all example sentences and explanatory notes were written independently rather than copied from textbook passages or exercises.

audit.scope: Unit 11 and 12 teaching pages, tables, illustrations, common-mistake and language-help boxes, exercises, and relevant answer-key entries examined for vocabulary coverage and grammatical distinctions.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA used where reliable; long collocations and expressions generally have empty IPA rather than speculative connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All fields are in English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Reviewed against study and exercise pages and printed answer key; checked original examples, sense/register notes, the reference JSON schema, IDs and conservative speech targets. No live browser import, recording playback or speech-recognition test was performed.
audit.limitations: No audio recordings are bundled. Successful live VocabLab import and browser TTS behaviour were not verified.

units.title: Unit 11 — At home
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 11. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Everyday life: accommodation, household spaces and objects
learningObjectives: Distinguish common British housing types such as detached, semi-detached, terraced and studio accommodation.
Name domestic spaces and differentiate attic or loft, cellar, basement, porch, patio and driveway.
Identify everyday objects and express their typical household uses.
Use natural household collocations with do, particularly washing-up versus washing, and avoid make housework.

sectionsChecked: A: Types of houses/places people live in
C: Everyday objects in the home

items.pt: casa isolada; casa que não é geminada
items.example: They bought a detached house with a garden on every side.
items.note: A house not physically joined to another house; detached is an important housing description in British English.

items.pt: casa em fileira; casa geminada em sequência
items.example: She lives in a terraced house between two neighbouring properties.
items.note: Joined to other houses in the same row; compare a semi-detached house and a detached house. American English often says row house.

items.example: My grandparents chose a bungalow because there are no stairs to climb.
items.note: In the British context, typically a home on one level, without an upstairs floor.

items.pt: casa geminada com apenas outra casa
items.example: Our semi-detached house shares one wall with the neighbours.
items.note: Joined to exactly one other house; informally a semi in British English.

items.pt: apartamento independente; apartamento com instalações próprias
items.example: The building has a self-contained flat with its own kitchen and bathroom.
items.note: The accommodation has its own essential facilities rather than sharing them with another household.

items.pt: casa pequena de campo; chalé rural
items.example: We rented a stone cottage in a quiet village.
items.note: A small house, typically in the countryside or a village; often older or picturesque.

items.example: He rented a studio flat where the bedroom and living area shared one space.
items.note: Normally a small flat with one principal room for sleeping and living; a bathroom is separate.

items.pt: casa grande com jardim; casa de férias em destino turístico
items.example: They rented a villa near the coast for their holiday.
items.note: The book gives both a substantial house with grounds and a holiday rental as typical senses.

items.pt: quarto principal; maior quarto da casa
items.example: The main bedroom overlooks the back garden.
items.note: Usually the largest or principal bedroom; the source also calls this a master bedroom, a term some speakers now avoid.

items.pt: quarto principal; suíte ou quarto principal (conforme o imóvel)
items.example: The estate agent described the largest room as the master bedroom.
items.note: Traditional housing term for the main bedroom; does not necessarily imply an en-suite bathroom. Many now prefer main or primary bedroom.

items.example: We keep the washing machine and freezer in the utility room.
items.note: A separate room for household equipment and chores, not usually a living room.

items.pt: depósito externo; barracão pequeno de jardim
items.example: The lawnmower is stored in a shed behind the house.
items.note: A small structure separate from the home, commonly used for tools and gardening equipment.

items.example: We found some old photographs in the attic.
items.note: The space just beneath a roof; it may be used for storage or converted into a room.

items.example: They turned the loft into a study.
items.note: In British housing, often synonymous with attic; loft can have other meanings in housing and architecture.

items.pt: adaptação do sótão para área habitável
items.example: A loft conversion gave the family an additional bedroom.
items.note: Building work that changes the roof space into usable accommodation, often with a new staircase.

items.example: The restaurant keeps its wine in a cool cellar.
items.note: Below ground level and often used for storage; contrast with a basement that is designed for living or working.

items.example: Her office is in a basement with windows onto the street.
items.note: A below-ground room or level, often used as living or working space; contrast with cellar.

items.example: The artist paints in a bright studio behind her house.
items.note: Here a workroom for an artist or photographer, not necessarily a studio flat.

items.pt: patamar da escada; área no topo da escada
items.example: Leave the spare towels in the cupboard on the landing.
items.note: A flat area at the top of or between flights of stairs; not a room or entrance hall.

items.pt: hall de entrada; corredor de entrada
items.example: Please leave your umbrella in the hall.
items.note: In domestic British English, often the space just inside the main entrance; hall also has other meanings.

items.example: The hallway leads from the front door to the stairs.
items.note: Entrance and passage space in a home; broadly similar to hall in this context.

items.example: We waited on the porch until the rain stopped.
items.note: A covered area immediately outside an entrance; not the same as a patio in the garden.

items.example: We ate breakfast on the terrace overlooking the garden.
items.note: Here an outdoor paved sitting area; terrace can also refer to a row of houses or levels of ground.

items.example: Their patio is large enough for a table and six chairs.
items.note: A paved outdoor area used for sitting or dining, often adjoining the house.

items.pt: entrada para carros; acesso de veículos à garagem
items.example: He left the car on the drive instead of putting it in the garage.
items.note: British English noun for the short private vehicle route from the road to a home; also called a driveway.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: I couldn't find the remote control, so I switched the television off manually.
items.note: Also commonly shortened to the remote in conversation.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Can you pass me the corkscrew to open this bottle?
items.note: A tool for removing the cork from a bottle, especially a wine bottle.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: I've packed my phone charger but forgotten the cable.
items.note: A device used to recharge a mobile phone battery; charger alone is common when context is clear.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Use the peeler rather than a knife to remove the potato skins.
items.note: Tool for removing thin skins from vegetables or fruit.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: We need another toilet roll for the bathroom.
items.note: British English for a roll of toilet paper; the roll is countable, while paper is often uncountable.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Cut the onions on a chopping board to protect the worktop.
items.note: British English; American English often uses cutting board.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Hang your jacket on a coat hanger in the wardrobe.
items.note: Also simply hanger; the full form specifies a hanger for clothing.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: I unfolded the ironing board before pressing my shirt.
items.note: A board used when ironing clothes; iron can have an unexpected pronunciation without an audible r.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Is there a socket beside the desk for my laptop?
items.note: Here an electrical power outlet; in American English often outlet.

items.pt: pá de lixo e escovinha; conjunto de pá e escova
items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Use a dustpan and brush to collect the crumbs from the floor.
items.note: Household cleaning tools used together to gather dust and small pieces from a floor.

items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: A fine grater works well for hard cheese.
items.note: Utensil for producing small pieces of food such as cheese or vegetables.

items.pt: jogo americano; apoio individual de mesa
items.section: C · Everyday objects in the home
items.example: Please put a table mat under your plate.
items.note: A protective mat for a place at the table; a heatproof mat can also protect a surface from hot containers.

items.pt: fazer tarefas domésticas; cuidar da limpeza da casa
items.example: We usually do housework together on Saturday mornings.
items.note: Use do rather than make with housework; the noun housework is uncountable.

items.example: I'll do the washing-up if you prepare dinner.
items.note: In British English, wash dishes after a meal; washing-up is not the same as doing the washing of clothes.

items.pt: lavar roupas; cuidar da roupa suja
items.example: She does the washing twice a week.
items.note: In this household context, washing means laundry rather than washing dishes.

items.example: I usually do the ironing while listening to a podcast.
items.note: Do the ironing is the usual collocation for this household task.

items.example: Could you do the hoovering before the guests arrive?
items.note: Informal British English, derived from the Hoover brand; vacuuming is a more general alternative.

items.example: They do the gardening early in the morning when it's cooler.
items.note: Natural phrase for gardening chores; use do for this listed household task.

items.example: I did the dusting before putting the books back on the shelves.
items.note: Remove settled dust from objects and surfaces; normally do the dusting.

items.example: My partner does the cooking, and I clean up afterwards.
items.note: Phrase for taking responsibility for preparing meals, rather than making a particular dish.

items.pt: entrada para carros; acesso da rua até a garagem
items.example: There's space for two cars in the driveway.
items.note: Alternative to drive for the private approach to a home, explicitly accepted in the answer key to Exercise 11.3.

items.example: We can watch the sunset from the balcony upstairs.
items.note: An elevated platform outside a room or building; the answer key mentions it as a possible alternative to patio or terrace.

items.pt: varanda coberta ao longo de uma casa
items.example: We sat under the verandah during the afternoon shower.
items.note: A roofed open-sided outdoor area attached to a building; the answer key lists this as a conditional alternative. Also spelled veranda.

items.pt: bancada de trabalho; bancada de cozinha
items.example: Put the chopping board on the kitchen worktop.
items.note: British English for a flat working surface in a kitchen; American English often says countertop. Appears in Exercise 11.4.

units.title: Unit 12 — Everyday minor problems
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 12. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Everyday life: household faults, minor injuries and mishaps
learningObjectives: Differentiate leaking, cracked, chipped, smashed, crushed and dented damage.
Describe failed devices or power supplies with run out, dead, power cut, break down, crash and flat battery.
Describe minor injuries with twist, bump, bang, bruise, trip and graze.
Use mislay, spill, stain, blocked, lock yourself out, and appropriate clock descriptions.
Recognise verbs that are also countable nouns and select common repair-related collocations.

sectionsChecked: A: Things that go wrong in houses and flats

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The pipe under the sink started to leak overnight.
items.note: Verb and countable noun: a pipe leaks, and you can discover a leak. Usually used about water, gas or other substances escaping.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: A football smashed the greenhouse window.
items.note: Stronger than crack or chip: usually break something violently or into pieces.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The glass may crack if you pour boiling water into it.
items.note: Verb and countable noun; a crack is a line of damage, while cracked describes the damaged object.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The vase is cracked, but it hasn't broken into pieces.
items.note: Damaged by a crack; contrast with chipped, which means a small piece has come off.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The batteries have run out, so the torch won't switch on.
items.note: Run out of something is also common when naming the supply: we've run out of batteries.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The radio doesn't work because the batteries are dead.
items.note: Dead describes batteries that have no usable charge; comparable to batteries that have run out.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: Be careful not to chip the edge of the plate.
items.note: Verb and countable noun: a chipped cup has a small piece missing, while a cracked cup has a line in it.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The mug is chipped near the rim, so please use another one.
items.note: Describes a small piece broken away, commonly from cups, plates and other hard objects.

items.pt: queda de energia; interrupção de energia elétrica
items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: We used candles during the power cut.
items.note: British English for a period without electricity; American English often says power outage.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The cupboard handle came off when I pulled it.
items.note: Usually something becomes detached unexpectedly; often interchangeable with fall off here.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: A button fell off my coat while I was travelling.
items.note: Something becomes separated and falls away; unlike come off, it explicitly suggests falling.

items.pt: quebrar; parar de funcionar (máquina ou veículo)
items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The washing machine broke down halfway through its cycle.
items.note: Intransitive for mechanical failure; past tense broke down. Not for a physically cracked plate.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The heavy books crushed the biscuits in my bag.
items.note: Damage by pressing with great force; crushed can describe fragile food that has been squashed.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: The crisps were crushed at the bottom of the shopping bag.
items.note: Past participle/adjective describing objects damaged by pressure; not the same as chipped or cracked.

items.section: A · Things that go wrong at home
items.example: My laptop keeps crashing whenever I open the editing software.
items.note: Here software or a computer stops working suddenly; crash has other meanings, including road accidents.

items.example: She twisted her ankle while walking down an uneven path.
items.note: An ankle injury caused by turning it awkwardly; your changes to my, his, her, etc.

items.example: I bumped my head on the low doorway.
items.note: Bump can be a verb or countable noun; often suggests an accidental impact that is not severe.

items.example: He banged his head against the cupboard door.
items.note: Bang often suggests a relatively forceful, sudden impact or loud noise; a bang is also a countable noun.

items.example: A large bruise appeared on my arm after the fall.
items.note: A dark mark caused by an injury without necessarily breaking the skin; bruise is also a verb.

items.pt: ficar com hematoma; machucar por impacto
items.example: I tend to bruise easily after minor knocks.
items.note: Verb: develop or cause bruising; as a noun, a bruise is the visible dark mark.

items.example: She tripped over a cable but managed not to fall.
items.note: Your foot catches on something and you lose your balance; often trip over something.

items.example: The child fell down on the pavement but wasn't seriously hurt.
items.note: Past fell down; falling can follow a trip but is not required for something to count as a trip.

items.pt: ralar o joelho; esfolar levemente o joelho
items.example: I grazed my knee when I slipped on the pavement.
items.note: A graze damages the skin surface; the book contrasts this with a bruise.

items.example: He cleaned the graze on his elbow with water.
items.note: Countable noun for a superficial injury; graze is also a verb with other meanings.

items.pt: guardar em lugar errado e não encontrar; perder temporariamente
items.example: I've mislaid my keys again, but they must be somewhere in the flat.
items.note: More precise than lose when you have put something somewhere and cannot find it; past and past participle mislaid.

items.pt: pen drive; dispositivo portátil USB de armazenamento
items.example: I saved the report on a memory stick before leaving the office.
items.note: British English term for a USB flash drive. It can be mislaid, but the source does not mean computer RAM.

items.example: Please don't spill coffee on the keyboard.
items.note: Verb and noun (a spill); for liquids accidentally escaping from a container. British past tense spilt or spilled.

items.example: There's a dark stain on the carpet where the tea was spilt.
items.note: Countable noun and verb; often a mark that is difficult to remove.

items.example: The berry juice may leave a stain on your shirt.
items.note: Natural collocation for a mark remaining after a substance contacts a surface.

items.example: The kitchen sink is blocked, and the water won't drain away.
items.note: A blocked sink or drain cannot carry water away; blocked can also describe roads or access.

items.example: Be careful not to dent the car door with your bicycle.
items.note: Verb and countable noun for a shallow hollow made by an impact; unlike a scratch, metal is pushed inward.

items.example: The garage estimated that the repairs would take two days.
items.note: Plural noun for fixing damage; the singular repair is also possible. Common phrase pay for the repairs.

items.example: The printer stopped working just before the meeting.
items.note: General expression for a device failing; unlike break down, it can describe almost any device.

items.pt: ficar trancado do lado de fora sem a chave
items.example: I locked myself out when I went downstairs to collect a parcel.
items.note: A reflexive phrasal expression; change yourself to myself, herself, ourselves, etc.

items.pt: não pega; não liga (motor ou veículo)
items.example: My car won't start on cold mornings.
items.note: Common phrase for a car or engine that fails to start; won't is not simply a refusal by a person.

items.example: The car wouldn't start because it had a flat battery.
items.note: British English expression for an exhausted battery; compare dead batteries in a torch.

items.example: The kitchen clock is five minutes slow.
items.note: For a clock or watch, slow means showing an earlier time than the correct time.

items.example: My watch is ten minutes fast, so the train hasn't left yet.
items.note: For a clock or watch, fast means showing a later time than the correct time.

items.example: The old wall clock stopped when its battery ran out.
items.note: Here a timepiece no longer runs; distinguish from a clock that is merely slow or fast.

items.word: What time do you make it?
items.pt: Que horas você acha que são?; que horas marca o seu relógio?
items.example: What time do you make it? My watch seems to be running slow.
items.note: Informal British English way to ask someone what time they think it is; make has a special meaning in this fixed question.

items.example: A sudden flood damaged several houses near the river.
items.note: The unit explicitly notes that flood is both a countable noun and a verb; flood often refers to an excessive amount of water.

items.example: The lock on the front door needs replacing.
items.note: Countable noun; lock is also a verb, as in lock the door or lock yourself out.

items.example: We called a plumber when the tap started leaking.
items.note: A tradesperson who installs or repairs water pipes and related equipment; the b is silent.

items.example: The mechanic found a problem with the car's starter motor.
items.note: Person who repairs machines or vehicles; central to Exercise 12.1.

items.pt: chamar; mandar buscar alguém para prestar ajuda
items.example: We had to send for an electrician when the lights went out.
items.note: British usage: ask a professional or someone to come; can be formal or a little old-fashioned in some contexts.

items.pt: chamar um profissional para atendimento no local
items.example: We called out a technician when the heating failed.
items.note: Call a professional to come and deal with a problem, often outside ordinary hours.

items.example: I'll fix the loose handle back on the drawer.
items.note: Reattach something that has come off; the central target is come off, while this variant is used in the exercise.

items.pt: queimar; deixar passar do ponto no fogo
items.example: I burnt the toast because I forgot it was under the grill.
items.note: In cooking, burn food makes it black or spoiled; past tense burnt or burned. Appears in the answer key to Exercise 12.1.

items.example: Too much salt can ruin an otherwise good meal.
items.note: Strong verb for damaging quality or usefulness; ruined is one of the combinations in Exercise 12.3.

items.example: The printer stopped halfway through because of a paper jam.
items.note: Specific printer failure mentioned in the suggested answer to Exercise 12.3.
